title: Unique Points (Hashable)

docs.title: Collection Types — Hash Values for Set Types

hints: Tuples can't go into a `Set`, but a struct can if it's `Hashable`.
Declaring `: Hashable` is enough — Swift synthesises `==` and hashing because both properties are `Int`.
`struct Point: Hashable { let x: Int; let y: Int }` and `Set(coords.map { Point(x: $0[0], y: $0[1]) }).count`.
jsBridge: JS `Set`s compare objects by **identity**, so two `{x:1,y:2}` objects are different. Swift compares by **value** through `Hashable`, and structs get `==` and `hash(into:)` synthesised automatically. Tuples can't conform to protocols yet, so they can't go in a `Set`.

compass.q: JS devs stringify keys (`${x},${y}`) to dedupe points. What does synthesised `Hashable` give you instead, and why is it safer?
Java requires overriding both `equals` and `hashCode` consistently. How does Swift synthesis prevent the classic "equal but different hash" bug?
If you hand-write `==` to compare only `x`, but keep the synthesised hash, what breaks?
SwiftUI `ForEach` and diffable data sources need `Hashable`/`Identifiable`. What happens when two items hash equal but aren't the same row?
